unit.title: Planetary Systems
unit.blurb: Galaxies and the Milky Way, how our Solar System formed from a nebula, asteroids, dwarf planets and comets, and Earth's magnetic shield.

O1.t: Describe a galaxy, the Milky Way and the main shapes of galaxies.

O2.t: Describe the Solar System, how it formed, and the asteroids, dwarf planets and comets in it.

O3.t: Explain why asteroids form a belt and why a comet's tail points away from the Sun.

O4.t: Describe how Earth's magnetic field is produced and how it protects life.

captions: Welcome to Atomic Education.
This lesson was written by the Atomic teaching team to
help you learn Cambridge Lower Secondary Science with confidence.
Let's begin!
Welcome to Unit 14: Planetary Systems.
The Universe is everything: all of space, time, matter and energy.
Looking at the night sky, you see cosmic history,
because starlight takes years to reach us.
But light pollution is hiding the stars.
On a truly dark night, you can see the Milky Way,
our home galaxy. It's a spiral galaxy, like a giant spinning pinwheel,
containing hundreds of billions of stars.
Our Sun is on one of its spiral arms,
about 27 thousand light years from the centre.
The Milky Way is one of trillions of galaxies.
It belongs to a Local Group of about 54 galaxies held together by gravity.
Our closest major neighbour, Andromeda, is heading our way,
but it will take about four billion years to arrive!
Galaxies come in different shapes.
Spiral galaxies like ours have arms.
Elliptical galaxies are oval, like rugby balls.
Lenticular galaxies are lens-shaped with a bulge in the middle.
Irregular galaxies have no defined shape.
A galaxy contains stars, planetary systems, gas and clouds of stellar dust:
tiny specks of ice, carbon, silicon, oxygen and metals.
Unlike house dust, it isn't skin and hair!
It blocks our view, but it's the building block of new planetary systems.
The Universe is also expanding.
Imagine galaxies as dots on a balloon being blown up:
they all move further and further apart.
Six dots are drawn on a balloon to stand for galaxies.
Then the balloon is blown up.
Predict: what will happen to the distances between the dots?
Pause and decide.
Watch. As the balloon is blown up, the dots start to move apart.
When the balloon is fully blown up,
every dot is further from every other dot,
and no dot is at the centre.
Explain what you saw.
The dots move apart because the rubber between them stretches.
In the same way, space itself is stretching,
so distant galaxies are moving away from us and from each other.
This is evidence that the Universe is expanding.
Pause and explain it in your own words.

captions: A planetary system is one star and all the
objects held in orbit around it by gravity:
planets, moons, comets, asteroids and tiny bits of ice and rock.
Ours is the Solar System, with the Sun at its centre.
Eight planets orbit the Sun in elliptical paths.
Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars are rocky planets; Jupiter, Saturn,
Uranus and Neptune are gas planets.
All except Mercury and Venus have moons.
Planets and moons are non-luminous: we see them because they reflect sunlight.
That's why stars twinkle but planets shine with a steady light.
Astronomers have found over four thousand other stars with planets, called exoplanets.
NASA's planetary fact sheet gives the time each
planet takes to travel once around the Sun,
measured in Earth years.
Mercury takes less than a quarter of a year, Earth takes one year,
and Mars almost two.
But Jupiter takes about 12 years and Saturn nearly 30.
Pause and decide: what is the pattern between a planet's distance from
the Sun and the time it takes to complete one orbit?
About 4.6 billion years ago, the Solar System formed from a nebula:
a giant cloud of gas and stellar dust.
Gravity pulled it inwards and it began to spin,
forming a hot protostar at the centre, which became the Sun.
Around it, dust and rock stuck together into protoplanets, which grew into planets.
Rocks left over became asteroids.
Most orbit between Mars and Jupiter, in the asteroid belt,
where Jupiter's strong gravity stopped them forming a planet.
Dwarf planets are bigger than asteroids but smaller than planets,
and gravity has rounded their shape.
Pluto was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006.
Beyond Neptune lies the Kuiper Belt, full of icy objects.
Comets are made of ice, dust and rock and follow very long,
thin orbits. Near the Sun, the ice turns to gas,
releasing dust that the Sun's radiation pushes into a tail.
So a comet's tail always points away from the Sun.

captions: Earth has a solid inner core and a
liquid outer core of molten iron and nickel.
This molten metal is always moving,
creating electric currents that produce a magnetic field.
So Earth's core acts like a giant magnet,
with a field reaching far into space.
The magnetic North pole isn't at the geographic pole,
and it wanders by tens of kilometres a year.
The field deflects the solar wind,
charged particles from the Sun that could strip away our atmosphere and harm life.
The solar wind also creates beautiful auroras, the northern and southern lights,
when its particles collide with atoms in the atmosphere and give out light.
And spacecraft can use solar sails, pushed by the solar wind,
to travel through space.
Now it is your turn to shine!
